title: Allah, the name itself
hookLine: the name itself, the one proper name, holding all the others

cards: Allahu akbar. One word sits inside every one of those phrases, and it hides so well in everyday speech that it's easy to stop hearing it.
A Muslim might say it many times before lunch without once asking: what kind of word is this? It isn't like the names still to come. Ar-Rahman describes.
Al-Malik describes. This one names. Before the names that describe, the name itself: Allah.

teach.h: THE PROPER NAME, NOT A DESCRIPTION.
teach.b: Muslim scholars call Allah al-ism al-'alam, the proper name, and some call it the greatest name. The other names describe Him: Allah is the Merciful, Allah is the King.

teach.h: THE ONE THE OTHER NAMES BELONG TO.
teach.b: The order never runs the other way: the names are said of Allah, and Allah is the one they all belong to. That's why, at the end of al-Hashr, the Qur'an can say He is Allah, and then pour out a string of names after it.
The name holds them. Where does the word come from? Here the grammarians disagree, and it's worth saying so.

Some said it comes from al-ilah, the god, the two words run together, so Allah means the God, the only one. Others said it isn't derived from anything at all: it's a name, full stop, never a common noun.
Both sides agree on some things.
It has no plural: there are ilahs, gods, but no plural of Allah.
It has no feminine. Grammar itself refuses to share it.

It's the name in the testimony, la ilaha illa Allah, there is no god but Allah. And it isn't only a Muslim word: Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews say Allah for God, and Arabic Bibles use it. Listen, too, to the sound.
Remember tajwid? The l in Allah is heavy and full when an a or u comes before it, as in Allahu akbar, and light after an i, as in bismillah. And the name ends in a soft h, almost just a breath.

how: Muslims say the name Allah throughout the day inside everyday phrases (bismillah, alhamdulillah, insha'Allah, Allahu akbar), and some repeat it on its own in dhikr, remembrance, often counting on prayer beads.

practice: On the in-breath, let the first part rise: al; on the out-breath, let the rest go, lah, and let the h at the end become just breath leaving you, so the name ends where the breath ends.
If you pray, you can let this be your remembrance; if you don't, simply listen to the sound and the breath together.

wordCard.voice: Allah. The proper name of God in Arabic, with no plural and no feminine, the name all the other beautiful names belong to. Today's word.
